Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old woman with several months of painful, dry, cracked palms (predominantly), with itching and intermittent scratching-related bleeding; occupational exposure as hotel housekeeper with inconsistent glove use suggests irritant/contact dermatitis; plan includes barrier protection, topical therapy, and close follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Soreness and cracking dry skin on the hands, mainly the palms; itchy at times; occasional bleeding with scratching.
- Timeline: Symptoms began ~3–4 months ago; gradually worsened; currently painful and affecting ability to work (hotel housekeeping).
- Exacerbating/initiating factors: Occupational exposure to cleaning products; occasionally wears gloves but not consistently; recent job change (~4 months ago) may be relevant.
- Associated symptoms: Itching; no fever, nausea, vomiting; no GI or urinary symptoms; appetite and general wellbeing preserved.
- Pertinent negatives: No systemic symptoms; no known allergies; no prior diagnosed skin disease reported; no ellergic reactions documented.

Past Medical History:
- Type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin).
- No documented prior skin conditions (eczema/dermatitis not diagnosed).

Medications:
- Metformin (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies: None noted.

Social History:
- Occupation: Hotel housekeeper; duties include cleaning of bedrooms, bathrooms, corridors.
- Gloves: Not consistently worn during cleaning.
- Smoking: Never smoked.
- Alcohol: A couple of pints per week.
- Other: Recently changed job; exposure to cleaning products at work.

Family History:
- Family history notable for diabetes.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Exam findings: Palms described as very cracked, dry, and itchy with scratching-induced bleeding; no other systemic findings reported.
- Additional notes: Not recorded beyond patient-reported exam finding.

Investigations:
- No labs or imaging mentioned.

Assessment & Plan:
- Overall Impression:
  - Working diagnosis: Dermatitis, most consistent with irritant contact dermatitis/hand dermatitis due to occupational exposure to cleaning products with inconsistent glove use. Allergic contact dermatitis is a consideration; general hand eczema remains plausible. Plan targets irritants, skin protection, and topical therapy.
- DDx Integration (brief):
  - Irritant contact dermatitis: Supported by occupational exposure, palm predominance, itching, cracking, and irregular glove use; no conflicting evidence.
  - Allergic contact dermatitis: Plausible given cleaning-agent exposure; patch testing could identify allergens; no direct evidence to confirm.
  - Hand dermatitis/eczema: Consistent with chronic dry, itchy hands and fissures; responds to steroids and emollients in many cases; no contradicting data.
  Note: No conflict noted between transcript and DDx.
- Issue 1:
  - Diagnosis: Irritant/contact dermatitis (hand dermatitis best fit given history and exam).
  - Plan: 
    - Advise strict glove use during cleaning at all times.
    - Apply topical corticosteroid to inflamed areas (specify regimen not in transcript; ensure prescription is provided).
    - Use stronger emollients several times daily (coat-on moisturizing for next 2 weeks).
    - Reassess in 1–2 weeks; if not improved or if spreading/worsening, return sooner.
- Issue 2:
  - Diagnosis: Occupational irritant exposure contributing to symptoms; potential allergic component.
  - Plan:
    - Consider patch testing if symptoms persist or recur after initial treatment to identify specific allergens.
- Issue 3:
  - Diagnosis: Xerosis with fissuring, possibly influenced by diabetes/metabolic dryness.
  - Plan:
    - Continue moisturization; address environmental factors; monitor for improvement.
- General plan:
  - Prescription to pharmacy for medications (topical corticosteroid, emollients) as discussed.
  - Education on trigger avoidance and skin care.
  - Follow-up appointment scheduled or advised in 1–2 weeks, earlier if symptoms worsen or spread.

Document Quality:
- Missing elements: No recorded vitals; no objective dermal photography or dermatology consult; no exact medication dosing or regimen documented beyond “topical steroid” and “stronger emollients.” Allergies explicitly stated as none, but cross-check recommended at next visit.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx aligns with transcript.
- Transcript quality: Clear and coherent; some minor details (exact steroid type/dose) not specified in transcript; plan remains consistent with stated management.

Notes:
- A prescription will be sent to the patient’s pharmacy for the indicated topical therapy and moisturizers; patient advised regarding the expected timeline (about 10–14 days) for initial improvement, with return if no improvement or if symptoms worsen.
